title: God in all things
hookLine: Ignatian spirituality finds God in all things

lines: A STUDENT AND A GRAMMAR BOOK.
WHEN DOES THE REAL PRAYER START?
cards: A young Jesuit student sits at a desk with a grammar book open, and he is worried. He joined to pray, and now his days are full of verb endings and lecture notes. When does the real spiritual life begin?

Ignatius's answer to students like him is not a longer hour in the chapel. Seek the presence of God in everything, he tells them: in conversation, in walking, in seeing, tasting, hearing, thinking, in all that they do.
The grammar book is not in the way. Today's phrase is the short form of that answer.

teach.b: God in all things. Four words that can sound like a greeting card, but in the Ignatian tradition they carry weight.

In the Contemplation to Attain Love, Ignatius asks the retreatant to consider how God dwells in creatures: giving being to the elements, life to the plants, feeling to the animals, understanding to people.

teach.h: GOD WORKS AND LABORS FOR US.
teach.b: Then a step further: God works and labors in all created things on our behalf. The world is not a stage set God left behind. It's a place where God is busy.
Saint Paul says it to the crowd in Athens, in the Douay-Rheims: "For in him we live, and move, and are."
In the guidance Ignatius wrote for Jesuits, he asks those in studies, who can't spend long hours in formal prayer, to find God in what's in front of them. A conversation can be a place of prayer.

teach.h: PRAYER IN A WALK, A MEAL, A PAGE.
teach.b: So can a walk, a meal, a page of hard reading. Two cautions keep this honest.
It doesn't mean everything is God: Catholic teaching keeps the Creator and the creature distinct; God is present in things, not the same as them.

teach.h: NOT EVERYTHING IS GOD. NOT EVERYTHING IS GOOD.
teach.b: And it doesn't mean everything that happens is good.

teach.h: IN HIM WE LIVE, AND MOVE, AND ARE.
teach.b: Ignatius also wrote the rules for discernment, because some movements lead away from God. Finding God in all things is a habit of attention, not rose-colored glasses.
It might mean noticing the steam off a cup of coffee, a coworker's patience, a child's question, and asking: where is God at work in this?

how: In the Ignatian tradition, people practice finding God in all things by paying attention to daily work, conversation and study as places of prayer, often looking back over the day in the examen.

games.q: what does “god in all things” mean?
o: a vow to pray for every living creature by name
a habit of noticing God at work in ordinary life
a blessing Jesuits say before every meal and task

p: God dwells and labors in creatures

games.q: you're a young Jesuit student. your days are full of lectures and you have little time to pray. what does Ignatius tell you?
o: drop the studies and pray longer.
look for God's presence in the studies themselves.
wait until the studies are done to pray.
games.why: he asks students to seek God in everything they do: talking, walking, seeing, thinking. the desk can be a place of prayer.

practice: Pick one thing in reach or in view, a cup, a window, your own hand, and look at it as if for the first time: its color, its weight, who made it. Then ask, without forcing an answer, how God might be at work in this one thing.
If you pray, simply say thank you for it; if nothing comes, the looking itself is the practice.

wordCard.voice: God in all things. The Ignatian habit of looking for God's presence and work in ordinary life, in study and talk and meals, not only in church. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: all things. Even a washed dish or a red light counts. See you tomorrow.
